speechtext:
May I join in congratulating both the mover (Mr. Hanna) and seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address. I think generally the house has been very fortunate over a number of years in having the address moved and seconded in a very satisfactory manner, and this year was no exception.
Before commenting at any length on the speech from the throne I should like to indicate what my objective is in making the comments that I am going to make. Some mention has been made, both in the House of Commons and outside it, regarding the responsibility of an opposition party. Some suggestion has been made that when the government has apparently abdicated its responsibility and refused to reveal its policies on particular matters, especially when those matters affect the national well-being, the opposition should adopt exactly the same kind of method. This, I noted, was the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) outside the house last night, and I noticed that it was the position taken again today in parliament.
Now, I could not disagree more with that position than I do. We in this group do not intend to remain silent until the government has announced its policy. We do not intend to be in the position of merely criticizing without having some positive proposals of our own to meet that kind of situation. Of course, the industrial disputes act could be amended, or new methods could be adopted by a conciliation board, and these points are worthy of our lengthy consideration. But they would not meet the immediate situation that confronts the Canadian people and the economy of Canada today. We believe that an opposition party worthy of the name must present to the Canadian people not only an alternative government, but it must present alternative policies that such a government would pursue. Anything less than that does not provide opportunities for the people of the country to make a real choice. We in this group have sought throughout the years to present real alternatives on any policy, that requires it, and

The Address-Mr. Coldwell this I believe to be the traditional parliamentary attitude generally wherever parliaments like ours exist, and is consistent with the tradition in this Canadian House of Commons.
Having said that, let me turn immediately to the railway strike. There is no doubt that any dislocation caused by a shut-down of traffic on the Canadian Pacific Railway will become increasingly serious as time goes on if the present situation is allowed to continue. There is no doubt, therefore, that it is in the national interest that railway operations should be recommenced as expeditiously as possible while another attempt is made to settle the differences between management and the employees.
That, it seems to me, was the desire of the Prime Minister in his closing remarks this afternoon. But I think we should go farther than waiting, as he suggested. A request should be made to both parties to recommence railway operations immediately on the basis previously existing, without prejudice to the rights of either side, and such a proposal is indeed reasonable. I believe that the C.P.R. employees will agree to this proposal. Indeed, they have already indicated that they would do so in a statement they issued two or three days ago, on January 7 to be precise. So far the C.P.R. management has refused, and if that refusal is continued-indeed I think the time has come now-the only alternative is for the federal government to appoint a controller to take temporary management of the C.P.R. and direct the immediate resumption of operations while further negotiations are continuing. I reiterate that this should be done without delay.
It is becoming increasingly apparent that the principal issue involved is the question of the management's desire to cease the employment of firemen on diesel engines in freight and yard services. On that issue the main disagreement between the company and the union, or its employees, is the question of safety. Now, the safety factor cannot be ignored either by this house, by the company, by the union or by the country. We in this House of Commons have a definite responsibility to the nation to make certain that any change which may subsequently be put into effect should completely safeguard the interests of the public in every particular.
Because the determination of this factor is really a technical question, it is a matter that should be investigated by an impartial board of inquiry comprised of experts and technicians that would hear and study representations concerning the safety and other factors involved in the removal of firemen from diesel freight and yard locomotives. Indeed, the


report of the conciliation board itself suggested some sort of survey after the proposed change had been made and in the light of experience gained. I believe it is the part of wisdom to conduct this inquiry first, particularly because the majority and minority reports disagreed on this point, and because of an obvious doubt even in the majority report which suggested that there might be reconsideration of the matter after a year's trial. I think we must take the doubts in the minds of the majority and the definite opinion of the minority into account.
The report of a board of inquiry such as we suggest should go to the mediation board thereafter appointed by the federal government, which would seek to mediate all issues remaining in dispute between the two parties, and seek to reach an agreement on the part of both parties. In the meantime, let me reiterate, the public interest requires the immediate resumption of the services over the C.P.R., and I believe it is the duty of this parliament to serve the public interest and to do indeed what we are suggesting.
Another important but separate problem never far from the minds of the employees of practically any industry you may name is the problem of automation. I am not saying that the problem of automation is specifically involved in the present railway dispute, but no government can stand idly by while the advent of this revolution in productive techniques creates certain crises in industry. There is no doubt that these new developments in production can be of great benefit to the community as a whole, but only if there is over-all planning to smoothly adjust the economy to the changes that are taking place or are anticipated. It is of little satisfaction to the worker if a magnificent new and technologically superior machine deprives him of his job and there is no other job to be found; nor is automation of much advantage to workers in industries, whether in factories, on the farms or in mines, if it deprives them of their means of life and of their markets.
Accordingly we think this is an opportunity for the federal government to consider this problem and no longer delay the appointment of a council comprised of representative employers, of trade unions, of government, of technical experts and other interests, to study and advise this house on the impact of automation, and to make sure that the new wealth that automation will make possible will be shared by all groups in the community. Intelligent approaches to all these problems should give authoritative advice on how best to promote the industrial, transportation and other changes involved in

new techniques without inconveniencing the community, as strikes do, or disrupting the community, which they also do, yet continuing the right of free men and women in a free society to give or to withhold their labour; for compulsion in this respect would destroy a fundamental principle of our democracy.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, may I turn to other matters which should receive consideration in this debate on the speech from the throne, even if some of them are not mentioned in that speech. There is one overall assessment which we must immediately make, and that is the revelation in the speech from the throne of the refusal, or the incapacity, of the government to deal with the needs of the common man and the common woman in our country. Economic expansion in Canada is pointed to, and there has been great economic expansion, but there is no awareness that large groups of Canadians do not share in the benefits of this great expansion. Take the case of the old age pensioner. There is no indication that old age pensions will be increased, in spite of the continued rise in the cost of living. No responsible person today would claim that the present old age pension is anywhere near adequate. Bearing in mind the substantial surplus which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is indicating he expects to be able to report to this house when he brings down the budget, the refusal of the government to do anything for the old age and other pensioners can be described as nothing less than callous.
The same judgment applies to the failure of the government to indicate improvements in social welfare generally. The steady processes of inflation, for which the government must assume its share of responsibility, have filched away the real value of the social welfare programs that have been announced with fanfare from time to time by the government and put into effect unanimously by members in this house, or indeed so almost unanimously that one can say unanimously. Therefore, although the speech from the throne refers to what it calls the excellent program of economic development in Canada, there is no doubt that those who are ill, those who are unable to work any longer because of age, are not sharing in this prosperity, but instead find that as the statistics of production climb, their lot by relativity becomes more and more unhappy.
Nor is there a single mention of health insurance in the speech from the throne. By the rigid limitations the government has set on its hospitalization program it has made the proposals it offered last year into
The Address-Mr. Coldwell a political football, and has even further postponed the carrying out of a pledge first made by the Liberal party 38 years ago. The failure of the government to act with resolution in this matter is, I think, unsupportable.
May I say to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) that while at the moment because of conditions that exist in certain countries we are able to bring to this country large numbers of desirable immigrants, yet one of the barriers hitherto against immigration to this country from the Scandinavian countries, the United Kingdom and other countries like them has been the lack of a comprehensive national health plan in Canada. I was told that authoritatively on several occasions when I was in northwest Europe during the autumn. When I suggested that we would like more people from the countries there I was told there were two reasons why we would not get them. One reason was, of course, that there was full employment, and the other was that the people understood that Canada had not social security measures which were sufficiently attractive to cause the people to emigrate to our country. In Britain I saw references to the lack of such measures here by people who had returned and who on one or two occasions gave their reasons for returning. After having been happy in Canada for two or three years illness came along and wiped out all their savings, and they had returned in order to get the benefits of the protection of the social security measures which they have there.
Health is one of the measures concerning which I felt there should have been discussion in this parliament even during the special session last November following the disposition of the international matters. I cannot adequately express my own disappointment that the government adjourned the session, thus preventing discussion on that occasion, nor can I adequately express my disappointment that when the speech from the throne came in there was no mention in it of national health insurance. I must say I expected it; in fact I was almost confident that something would be done in this regard at this session of parliament to at least bring proposals before the house so that when the provinces were willing and able to come under such a plan the plan would be available to them.
The speech from the throne also ignores the continuing chronic crisis in Canadian agriculture. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave some interesting figures this afternoon but they do not meet the situation nor do they meet the criticism that there is

The Address-Mr. Coldwell a chronic crisis in our agricultural economy. I have not ceased to deal with this in the house whenever the opportunity arose, but the government has rigidly refused to take the action necessary to enable agriculture to participate equitably in the benefits that the improvements in technology and other developments generally are bringing to Canada as a whole.
I know that even outside of the agricultural sector the gains in the economy are shared inequitably and unfairly but in agriculture, of course, the problem is more lasting and severe. I have only to read the financial sections of the daily newspapers to find concrete indications of the large increases in the profits of various corporations and the dividends that are being paid, increases that are not matched by the people who are, after all, the real and continuing producers of wealth whether they work in offices, in mines, in factories, on the farms or go down to the sea and fish. There is no doubt but that the cream of the so-called prosperity is being skimmed off by privileged groups in this country. I say to the Minister of Finance that there is something fundamentally wrong in the Canadian economy when in the midst of relative prosperity one of the basic industries of this country continues in a chronically depressed state.
Agriculture has suffered a severe and prolonged decline in its income, but it has not been as the result of lower production. This afternoon the Prime Minister produced some figures which I do not have but in 1955, the latest year for which complete statistics are available, the physical volume of agricultural production was actually higher than that of eight out of the 12 years between 1941 and 1954 and, indeed, as much as 30 per cent higher than in some years. A preliminary estimate indicates another increase in the index of farm production in 1956 as was suggested this afternoon; yet the real net income to the farmer in 1955 was lower than in any year since 1941 except 1954. I have the dominion bureau of statistics table before me which substantiates the statement I have just made. Indications are that the real net income in 1956 may be better, but not substantially better and certainly not better than in many of the years between 1941 and 1955.
It is a tragedy that in many cases the more successful a Canadian farmer is in giving the best of his talents to the production of food the lower becomes his income, his real return. As I have said, frequently the more successful a farmer is in increasing production and the more generous climatic factors are, the more serious the crisis he faces as far as income is concerned. Abundance in this economy is punished and scarcity is rewarded.


That, I submit, is a sense of values which indicates an outmoded economy. It is the sense of values of great monopolistic concerns which derive their profits from the economy of scarcity rather than the economy of abundance. I think we in this house do not immediately share that conception of such an economy; yet it is the economy that we permit to continue existing. So from time to time we find shivers of apprehension running through even my hon. friends of the Liberal government whenever reports come in of a big crop in western Canada or a heavy yield of apples in Nova Scotia or British Columbia, more potatoes in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick or more cattle in some other parts of Canada. When Providence has been generous there is a crisis in the air; there is worry and concern instead of rejoicing; there is inaction instead of programs designed to distribute the bountiful gifts of Providence to the people who need them.
In other words the farmer is suffering a depression because in a world where many children-yes, even in some parts of Canada -do not get enough milk, there has been too much milk; because in a world where two-thirds of the people go to bed hungry every night, there is too much bread; because where many old age pensioners have not enough income to buy all they would like in the way of changes of diet there have been on occasion too many peaches, too many apples and indeed too many potatoes. We in the C.C.F. say that a society which is unable to turn abundance to the service of the people is morally bankrupt and the government that stands idly by deserves the strongest censure. I cannot for a moment accept the dictum of some so-called private enterprisers that an economy of scarcity is better than one of abundance, and that two loaves of bread can be of less real value than one.
We have suggested many changes in policy that should be made. Precious years have been lost when the government instead of opposing the world food bank at United Nations could have been fostering it. If they had done so and if that bank had come into existence, we would then have had an effective international program for the disposal of our so-called agricultural surpluses.
The government's price support program initially was a measure to ensure that farm prices would bear an equitable relationship to the cost of things which the farmer had to buy, but this has proved to be a sham and a deception in many cases. It is certainly better than nothing, but it has not even begun to meet the promise made by a Liberal prime minister in 1944. At that time our farmers were expending their energies to produce but

were taking perhaps lower prices than they might have got for the products they were producing, and Mr. Mackenzie King made this statement:
If, to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to ensure them against an agricultural depression after the war.
I am not contending that we have the world-wide depression which was foreshadowed at the United Nations in 1945, or that that is what Mr. Mackenzie King had in mind, although it may have been. In any event he made that promise, and the fact is that today agriculture is a depressed industry. The agricultural depression is here and has oeen here for some time. We know now how quickly that solemn promise was forgotten.
Vigorous government action is needed to establish a parity price program for agricultural products to ensure a fair and adequate return for the produce of the farm, for the produce of our agricultural industry. A comprehensive plan of crop insurance is required. The P.F.A.A. is a good start, but I should like to see a comprehensive plan such as we have been advocating for the last 25 years.
Cash advances on farm-stored grain are needed and are warranted under the circumstances which now exist. National marketing boards should be established where requested by producers for all farm products entering into interprovincial and export trade. I am not advocating interference with provincial rights when I suggest that. Long-term commodity agreements and the acceptance of sterling in part payment for Canadian produce sold in sterling area countries are necessary. We could not accept full payment in sterling but we could accept part payment in sterling.
The Canadian government should announce a permanent national food and fibre policy which would have the objective of ensuring that the means of obtaining sufficient food and clothing for basic adequate standards would be placed within the reach of every Canadian, and that wherever possible temporary surpluses of agricultural commodities should be used as an important step toward feeding the hungry people of the world. I believe that by feeding the hungry people of the world, and by enabling them to feed themselves by the provision of machines and other aids, we can meet the threat of communism better than in any other way.
These are some of the elements of a dynamic policy to deal with Canada's agricultural crisis. There should be in effect a national farm policy which would attempt to integrate 82715-4
The Address-Mr. Coldwell the production, price and distribution problems more effectively into the rest of the economy.
Other questions are of immediate concern to this house at this time. I have referred to the effect that inflation has had upon the purchasing power of the dollar since the end of the war. These forces are again reasserting themselves. All of us are aware that inflation benefits large corporations the most because profits rise more than anything else. On the other hand those who are on fixed incomes, like pensioners, find their financial position severely affected. The farmers' plight too is made even more severe by inflation. The farm price-cost squeeze is made even more evident and apparent. The government claims to be adopting certain measures to deal with these forces. It is asserted that certain monetary measures have been taken to influence the flow of credit in this country. How effective they are remains to be seen, but certainly the government is not exercising the positive role which is necessary.
It has long been felt that one of the prime functions of the Bank of Canada when it was originally set up by the Bennett government-incidentally, at the strong urging of the C.C.F. and those who organized this movement-it has only finally won the reluctant support of the Liberal government-was to perform just that function, in part at least. We have been told that one of the means by which the central bank can affect the flow of credit in the country is through the use of the rediscount rate. Yet we had the admission of the Minister of Finance during the special session that the rediscount rate is being determined practically automatically by the chartered banks.

In any event the central bank was supposed to do what is not being done by the government at this time. I do not think any other conclusion can be reached but that the government is permitting the banks to determine the monetary policy of this country. Surely this has made of the Bank of Canada something of a shadow of what it was intended to be when this parliament passed legislation to establish it some years ago.
Let us see what have been some of the results of the policy which has been pursued. An increase in the interest rate bears most heavily on those sectors of the population least able to afford it. It has not restricted investment generally, but it has had the effect of sharply curtailing the funds available for housing and of sharply increasing the cost to thousands of people throughout Canada who had hoped to obtain the homes they needed.
The provinces and municipalities, too, faced with the heavy burden of extending public utilities and building more schools and hospitals, have found that a sharply increased interest rate has drastically increased their costs and their commitments. Many years ago we saw provinces inviting investors to invest in bonds yielding 5 per cent or better, and many municipalities were paying rates of 5 per cent or better. That is true again of many of the larger municipalities and some provinces, and I do not know what the smaller municipalities are going to do. These provinces and municipalities face an increasingly serious crisis.
Clearly what is called for is a series of selective controls directing investment into those fields most socially useful, and certainly housing, hospitals and schools should have the top priority in this field. We have long advocated, and it was in the Liberal platform for several elections, that we should establish a national investment board to achieve what I have just suggested. We should not permit the planning of development of this country to be done on the basis of the ability of people to pay a high interest rate. I do not think that is a proper or fair method to employ.
There is another problem that has been completely ignored by the government and which was touched upon this afternoon by both the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister. That is the phenomenally large deficit on current account of $1,002 million that Canada has in its trade balance for the first three quarters of 1956, as compared with $437 million for the same period in 1955. This deficit has been met-and again the Prime Minister indicated this this

afternoon-only by the heavy inflow of United States funds for investment in this country. We are put in a dangerous position by this situation. The government may think we now have little to fear. It may be inclined in its complacency to postpone taking the decisions that must inevitably be taken. Canada's trade cannot forever be balanced by this import of capital. The time will inevitably come when the inflow will decrease or the payment of interest and dividends on these investment funds will exceed the amount coming in. That is the time, possibly some years hence, perhaps sooner than we think, when the people of Canada will regret the failure of its government at an earlier time to take the steps necessary to place Canada's trade in a more stable position.
Our failure to develop better trading relationships with the commonwealth countries will, I believe, bring serious results. It is one of the factors, I am sure, that is causing Britain to look for closer association in the new system of trade which has been talked about a great deal in western Europe. That development, if Canada does not enter into special relationships with it-and we should make efforts at this early stage to ensure that we do-may very well leave our trade even more concentrated in the United States market with all the implications that threaten the independence of action of the Canadian nation even in political affairs as well as development. I realize that this European system will take some time to put into effect, but I feel that Canada should now be considering the possibilities by which we can be associated with it when it comes into effect.
I have always regretted that the Canadian government did not press more strongly for the establishment of a permanent international trading agency within the United Nations after the war. The international trade organization envisaged then was to bring to reality the vision of practical planning on the international level. The international trade organization was to deal with tariffs. It was to deal with commercial policy, economic development, commodity policy and, of course, cartels and agreements of a similar sort. Had Canada and other countries pressed more strongly for some such agency I believe Canada's trading position would be healthier. Canada should continue to work for some such system, but in the meantime there is no excuse for not having adopted such planning in our trading policies as has from time to time been suggested from this corner of the house.

Lest I forget it before I conclude what I wish to say, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis):
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "the rights of parliament'', the following words:
"and by reason of their failure to announce legislation establishing a comprehensive and nationwide program of health insurance, with provision for provincial participation."
I have been critical of what the speech from the throne contains and perhaps more particularly of what it does not contain. However, in conclusion I want to change the tune a little and commend the government for some of the things that are in the speech from the throne. I am glad indeed to see that it foreshadows financial aid through the provinces to the municipalities. I am very glad to see that aid is to be given to the universities that will participate in the plan, and like others in the house I regret that one of our great provinces has not seen fit to accept what I think is a proper offer of assistance to our universities from the government of Canada.
I think it is being more clearly shown from day to day and, indeed, was indicated in the example the Prime Minister gave in his speech this afternoon of the co-operation between the two language groups, that there is no desire to interfere with the control under the constitution of those matters that are placed within the right of the provinces.
I was very happy indeed to see this provision in the speech from the throne and to note that at last something is going to be done for our universities.
I am also glad to note that a Canada Council is to be established. I have long felt that we could do much in this country through a Canada Council to promote scholarships. However, I do not think that what is suggested is in any way adequate, nor will the grants to the universities provide adequate funds to do what is needed for our young people in order to provide them with the opportunities that I found-I say "I found"- are afforded to young people in the United Kingdom and some other western European countries to achieve the educational training and standing that will enable them to play a decisive part in their countries.
I was happy to see, too, that a committee is to be set up in the other place to study land utilization. I hope they will not overlook irrigation, and I hope they will not overlook flood areas that need to be drained. Particularly do I hope they will not overlook the South Saskatchewan river plan, which I believe would be of a great benefit to a large area within one of our prairie provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my comments on His Excellency's address I should like to offer my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I commend particularly the hon. member for Edmonton South, whose speech in my judgment was informative, moderate in tone and statesmanlike in quality.
In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne is almost barren of any proposals offering relief for the average Canadian from the harassing problems which have been hounding him during the past several years. The little man has been almost completely forgotten by the government, unless it can be argued that providing him with culture is an achievement worthy of being called relief. I can hardly appreciate the government's concern about providing culture to the Canadian people while those same people are allowed to languish under a dog eat dog policy that keeps them worried stiff and in the grip of fear from one week to another, fear lest their incomes may not be stretched over the needs of food, clothing and shelter. I believe, I think as much as does anyone in the house, in encouraging cultural pursuits for all Canadians, but there are such things as priorities. First I think we should do something to bring old age pensions, war veterans allowances and like social security measures into line with prices as they have risen in this country.
I very much commend the government for its decision to appropriate a further amount of money to be distributed by the Canada Council for assisting our Canadian universities in some of their construction projects. The Canadian universities have been having a fairly hard time. It is also worthy of commendation that the government is preparing to double the annual grants to the Canadian universities, and that these increased funds will be paid to the National Conference of Canadian Universities to be divided by them amongst the recognized institutions of higher learning. That is something it seems to me can be classed as a worthy project and one which, if the appropriations are substantial enough, will bring much-needed relief to the universities that are overcrowded and understaffed at a time when enrolments are rising swiftly.

The Address-Mr. Low
However, if this provision to help the universities could be accompanied by some substantial measure of help to worthy students through scholarships and bursaries, and extended into the high school area, then it would seem to me that we would be making the kind of progress in higher education that is so much needed to meet the challenge of these times. In the judgment of any Social Crediter, no monetary consideration should be allowed to stand between any capable and determined student and the greatest measure of higher learning that he wishes to attain. Our country is always richer and better off every time our universities and high schools turn out a truly educated and skilled Canadian.
I must also commend the government for the proposal to increase the federal grants to provincial governments in aid of technical and vocational training. I support all these proposals wholeheartedly, and I urge the government to be generous in the amounts they provide in each case.
I should like to say just a word about that section of His Excellency's address which deals with the entrance into Canada of Hungarian refugees. I think the government did well to send the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration over to Europe to study the situation at first hand so he would know exactly what to do about relieving Austria of the extremely heavy burden of looking after the refugees who had gone across the border into that country. His personal appearance on the scene in Europe will also help decide how far Canada can go in helping to relieve the suffering of these patriots who have demonstrated that they love liberty even more than they love life.
Canada is short of labour. That is one of the reasons given for rising costs of living and of materials. We in this country need skills of every kind. It would therefore seem to me to be foolish in the extreme to be too selective at a time like this about our immigration. We should receive into Canada as many of these patriots as we can possibly integrate into our society, using care only to screen out any possible subversives. In addition to that, since many thousands of Britons are now making application for permanent entry into this country, we should do everything we can to provide them with transportation to Canada on an equal basis with the Hungarians, and to provide employment for them when they get here.
I hope the government is stretching every resource in both of these worthy projects. I know that it is going to tax our housing accommodation to the very limit temporarily, but I am also sure that the Canadian people

from one end of this country to the other will respond wholeheartedly to the government's appeal for assistance in providing the new immigrants with homes. Canada needs to increase her population as rapidly as it is safe to do so. Some of our problems will never be solved until Canada has 25 million, 30 million or 35 million people.
Having said those things I now return to something I said to begin with, namely that the speech from the throne hardly mentions any one of a dozen or more serious problems that are besetting the Canadian people and have been giving them trouble for quite a long time. To be specific, may I say that I was amazed that the speech gives only passing reference to one of the worst tragedies that has struck our country for a long time.
I refer, of course, to the Canadian Pacific Railway strike. A great deal has been said this afternoon about it. I was not at all satisfied with either the contribution made by the Leader of the Opposition or that made by the leader of the government. It is tragic in the extreme, it seems to me, that at this time of year, in the dead of winter, the wheels of the great Canadian Pacific Railway should be brought to a full stop.
It must be remembered that in many important parts of our country the Canadian Pacific Railway has had almost a total monopoly on transportation for many years. The whole of the southern part of my province from Calgary south to the international border is served by only one railroad, namely the Canadian Pacific. There are a good many communities in that area and in other areas in Canada, including the maritime provinces, that are running dangerously low in their supplies of fuel and food. Wheat and livestock are not being moved. Hence the farmer's chance of getting even a small supply of cash with which to meet his living costs has been utterly destroyed. The farmer has already had to carry a much heavier burden than he ought to have been called upon to carry, considering the tremendous contribution he has made to the economy of this country for so many years.
I think the grounds on which the strike was called were rather slim, and certainly not important enough to justify the complete tie-up of the whole Canadian Pacific system. I am not trying to direct the blame against either the labour unions or the railway company. Undoubtedly the union people fear the results of automation. This alone should indicate to the government how important it is that some new policy be adopted which will guarantee the distribution amongst the consumers of Canada of an adequate supply of purchasing power in spite

of any rapid extension of mechanization and industry. The government has not done anything whatever to modify its policy to meet this growing trend toward automation which is bound to dislocate the labour forces of Canada, at least in its first stages. In the long run automation, in my judgment, will be a blessing to mankind; but for some years it could easily be a grave threat to security and a cause of fear unless steps are taken to make up for the lack of consumer purchasing power which will result from the process-that is, to make up that shortage- by a direct issue to the consumers of this country.
It is absolutely imperative, in my judgment and in our judgment here, that the railway start running again as quickly as possible. The first responsibility of this parliament should be, by whatever means lies in its power, to get the C.P.R. into operation. At the same time the outstanding matter of dispute between the railway and the firemen and engineers should be referred to a commission for study. That commission should, as quickly as possible, investigate every angle of the situation, and particularly the safety factor in the operation of freight trains and yard engines; and when the commission's decision is handed down it should be considered as binding on both parties. It seems to me that there is too much inclination to try to maintain the status quo at all costs. In matters of this kind there must be a disposition to find the right answer even if it means some compromise.
In the United States I understand that they have a board or commission that is called the presidential fact-finding board. I understand that board can be used for just such cases as we now have in our country. When the board is named, I understand that no strike is permitted. In other words, let the men go back to work. Then, the board must get busy at once and complete its investigation within a specified period of time. If I am not mistaken the board's decisions, when handed down, are considered final and binding upon both parties. I only point that out to indicate that there is a precedent in other countries for such a commission or board as has been suggested. I am certain that something will have to be done as soon as possible to get this railway running, even if it means the appointment of such a board.
I think the railway are to be commended for trying to discover ways of cutting down costs and effecting savings wherever they can. They are placed in a most difficult position. On the one hand the Canadian people, especially those in the western provinces that stand at the very peak of the
The Address-Mr. Low freight rate structure, are demanding a reduction in the heavy and discriminatory freight rates that exist. They point out that since 1945 these freight rates have more than doubled. The farmers, especially in western Canada, are forced to pay freight costs both ways, on the goods they buy that come from eastern Canada and on the goods they sell that go to the head of the lakes or to the seaboard. You cannot blame them, therefore, for demanding lower freight rates, and in turn if they demand lower freight rates the railway must effect savings. Who is to say, therefore, that the railway is wrong in trying to effect these savings?
According to western Canadian thinking the government has been seriously lacking in courage in connection with this whole strike from the beginning. Certainly the government has not shown very much disposition to get the railway running again; that is clear. It is clear also that the nearness to a general election has made them timid and diffident in dealing with a situation like this. This is a time for courage and vision. I am positively certain that there were ways and means during the past few weeks by which the: disastrous work stoppage on the Canadian Pacific could have been avoided, but it was not avoided and somebody has to take the responsibility for it. As I said, the important thing now is to get the railway running again, and Social Crediters are prepared to back the government in whatever measures may be taken to accomplish that end and to provide for a thorough study of the dispute outstanding between the two sides. Let me also say that when a mutually satisfactory commission does hand down a decision, that decision should be binding on both parties.
We must not follow any policy, Mr. Speaker, that will deny to industry the opportunity to improve its processes and give better service to the Canadian people at lower cost; that is fundamental to our thinking. The future and its needs are going to demand improvements in all our industrial processes and lower costs. Certainly it can be said with perfect truth that the technological advances that have been made over the years, and that are now being made, are not resulting in the reduction of costs to the Canadian consumer. There is a reason for that, and we ought to find that reason and correct it. Automation is fast replacing labour in many fields. It is going to be necessary for labour to find employment in other fields. This in itself gives rise to considerable fear on the part of the working man. There is a fear that the Canadian Pacific Railway, for example, may be inclined to place the names of presently unneeded workmen on the call board along with many

The Address-Mr. Low other names, and that it will become a stagnant board with a great many names and few calls for some of the persons whose names are on that board. That is a real fear on the part of railwaymen.
There is a fear also lest they be cut off with no jobs at all. A suggestion has been made that in cases of this kind, and for those who may be affected in the future, certain financial assistance should be extended for a period of six months or until such time as the displaced workmen can be absorbed into some other industry. Perhaps though, with a provision of that kind, some effort should be made to provide training for the displaced workmen so they can readily find employment in some other field. Those are suggestions that can be considered and will have to be considered as the months wear on and more mechanization comes into our industry.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to turn for a few minutes to some of those problems I mentioned that have been harassing Canadian people for a long time and from which little or no relief appears to be indicated in government policy in the speech from the throne. I think the one which most plagues the Canadian people as a whole and which causes them more distress than anything else is the continuously rising cost of living. Recent announcements from the bureau of statistics show that the cost of living index stands at 120.4 in terms of the new method of expressing it. This is an all-time high. When it is converted into terms of the pre-1949 index, in December it would have stood at 193.4, that is in relation to 100 for the 1935-39 period. The speed with which the index rose during the autumn months of 1956 startled the Canadian people. Most of the people with whom I came into contact in travelling across the country expressed alarm at the prospect that they feared we would have to expect for the next six months. There seems to be every evidence now that nothing we can do will prevent a further rise of several points in the cost of living index between now and July of this year.
There is not a single word, however, to be found about that situation in the speech from the throne. You would think the government would have something to say about a matter as important as that, impinging as it does very heavily upon the welfare of the people.
I do not wish to attempt, by any means, to throw all the blame for the situation on the government. I know there are many factors entering into this increasing price and cost of living structure. But the people of Canada will judge the government on its policies, and of course they will do that within the next few months when the government goes


to the country in a general election. There is no doubt in my mind, however, that government policy has not only failed to come to grips with the problem of the rising cost of living and provide relief for the Canadian consumer, but actually government policy has contributed to a great extent to the spiralling of costs. The government is inclined, of course, to shrug off the whole nasty situation by saying we are suffering from inflation caused by an unprecedented rate of capital expansion. There is some truth to that, of course, but only some.
It is generally conceded, Mr. Speaker, that inflation means too much money chasing after too few goods. Now, in the light of that is the present situation in Canada real inflation? I want to examine that for just a moment or two. First let us take a look at the supply of goods available to the consumers of this country. The September, 1956, statement of inventories, shipments and orders in the manufacturing industries issued by the dominion bureau of statistics contains some very interesting tables. I want first of all to look at this table found on page 4 of the report, where one finds estimated the stocks on hand for every month from January, 1952, to September, 1956. The table shows that the total of all inventory held by manufacturing industries in Canada as of September, 1956, was $4,578,805,000. That was the highest total inventory of any month certainly since 1952, and I am satisfied that if I could get all the facts going back over the years I could venture to say the highest in Canada's history.
Of this total inventory held by the manufacturing industries there are three divisions; raw materials, goods in process of manufacture, and finished products.

I said September, 1956. In every one of these three divisions the total at September, 1956, was considerably in excess of the total in any preceding month except for a $5 million decline in raw materials from August to September of 1956, but that is a negligible amount and it can be attributed to the seasonal changes in arrangements. There is also a slight decline in the goods in process from June, 1956, to September of the same year, which again is negligible. Both of these can be attributed, as I said, to seasonal fluctuations, which are only natural. The general trend has been continuously upward, and we now have on hand in Canada over $4J billion worth of goods held by the manufacturing industries of this country.

Now, in the consumer goods industries the total inventory at the end of September of 1956 reached $1,093,138,000, a total that is higher than at any other time since 1952, and very likely higher than at any previous time in our history. A similar statement can be made of perishable goods. In petroleum and coal products the inventory at September last was the highest in history. In electrical supplies, although there was a slight decline in the three months from July, 1956, to September, yet the inventory at September, 1956, was $15 million over that for December, 1955, and $133 million over that for January, 1952.
Even in the iron and steel products industries the total inventory at September was $841,666,000, a figure greater than at any time since 1952. There was some decline in the finished products division of this particular industry, but both goods in process and raw materials on hand were greater in value than at any time since 1952. And this is the particular division where this country is supposed to have the serious shortages. The figures successfully dispute that claim.
I will not weary the house with many more figures, but I think I should say just a word about the capital goods industries lest someone here finds reason in that section to claim that we are actually suffering a shortage of goods. The total inventory in the capital goods industries at September, 1956, was $391,335,000, which is greater than at any time since 1952, and very likely the greatest of all time.
Let us turn for a moment to the money supply of our country, which is the other angle to the situation. The total money supply in 1954 was $11,276,900,000, while at September of 1956 it was $12 billion, in round figures. This shows a very small increase in the total money supply available to the public with which to buy a very greatly increased production. Let us not forget that at September, 1956, our gross national production was running at the rate of $29 billion a year, while in 1954 it reached only about $25 billion.

It was running at approximately $25 billion in 1954. I think I am quite right. In the light of these facts it is perfectly clear to me that the present high cost of living cannot be blamed on real inflation, too many dollars chasing far too few goods. Especially is this conclusion given real backing when we consider that there has been a slackening off in production in certain much-wanted
The Address-Mr. Low goods in this country. That slackening off has reached quite serious proportions in the last six months.
I was attracted to an article that appeared recently in the Calgary Herald concerning a great industry in this country. It appeared in the issue dated October 25, 1956. The heading of the article is "Lay-Offs Hit B.C. Lumbering". This is the pertinent story:
Labour and management officials in the British Columbia timber industry have forecast widespread unemployment in the industry this winter.
Both groups agreed it would be "the worst winter since the war" and some said unemployment might spread to other industries.
International Woodworkers of America expect to have 1,200 men out of work by mid-November. Already nearly 800 have been laid off.
That was back in October. There are more than that now. The article goes on to say:
"I cannot remember losing 1,200 men in such a short time", an I.W.A. official said.
"In nine years experience I have never seen so many men looking for work as there are now."
Further on in the article, Mr. Speaker, we find the following:
Officials agreed that sawmill workers will be hit first.
Two reasons given for the expected slump are:
Attempts by the government to control inflation by clamping down on new home mortgages, thus reducing the demand for new houses.
High shipping costs which have caused the United Kingdom to reduce orders from Canada and start buying more common grade timber from Russia and the Baltic countries.
A spokesman said the industry will have to consider asking Ottawa to lift the mortgage restrictions.
I point that out only to indicate the truth of what I said a moment ago and to give backing to it. At a time when we are actually slackening off production in the country, not only in the lumber industry but in certain others, how in the name of common sense anyone can cling to the old story that we are suffering real inflation I cannot understand.
There is another fact, Mr. Speaker, which I think we all ought to take into account as we consider this particular subject of the cost of living and what to do about it. The dominion bureau of statistics figures indicate clearly that in 1955 the Canadian people piled up a total of $26,600 million worth of goods and services. I think that was the figure mentioned a moment ago by the Minister of Finance. In that same year, 1955, the distribution of purchasing power amongst the consumers of this country fell so far short of being enough to enable the Canadian people to buy and consume what they had produced, if they wanted it, that they were forced to run charge accounts, to buy on instalment credit and to borrow in the form of cash personal loans from the

The Address-Mr. Low banks and small loan companies the staggering total of $2,600 million. These are the facts as supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics. In other words, the Canadian people in 1955 had to mortgage future incomes to the extent of more than $2J billion in order to be able to consume the goods they had produced. Does that indicate, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, too much money chasing after too few goods? I maintain that it shows just the opposite and the situation for 1956, when all the facts are in, will indicate a similar picture, if not one that is worse.
What, then, is causing the continuous increases in prices and in the cost of living? It certainly is not inflation, according to the accepted meaning of the term. Economists are finding it necessary to coin new phrases and terms to describe it. They are calling it a wage-price spiral. This spiral was set in motion on the one hand by the government itself in its demands for manpower and materials. It is competing with private industry for both manpower and materials that are available. It is true that the one real shortage we find in this country is in certain types of labour, unless one calls a lack of brains and vision on the other side of the house a shortage. I think perhaps that will have to be considered, brains and vision to meet the situation as we face it today.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And courage.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And courage. We in the opposition for quite a number of years now have been urging the government to take swift and sure action to guard against the contingency that is now arising. In fact it is getting worse from day to day. We have advocated a far more realistic immigration policy that would increase the labour supply in those divisions where a shortage was indicated, or was developing; but the government did nothing about our proposals, or very little. The people of Canada will undoubtedly have this in mind when they weigh the government in balance in the next few months. There is no doubt that if courage and vision had been exercised since the war the present wage-price spiral would not have developed.
When that spiral began to assume serious proportions it appears that the government became panicky; they budgeted for a revenue surplus for this year to restrict the money supply. That surplus will likely reach more than $300 million by the end of this fiscal year. Moreover, the government and its agencies together took monetary action to bring about a blanket restriction of credit. The government have been exceedingly evasive about what they have done in this


field thus far. They have refused to give the house the information that it requires to properly assess the situation.
The fact is, however, that this government has established a short term treasury bill rate of around 3J per cent, which unquestionably has been the snake in the grass in this whole rise in the interest rate which has had such undesirable effects upon our whole economy. The Bank of Canada quite properly felt it could not maintain a rediscount rate lower than the government's own short term treasury bill rate. The chartered banks then used this rediscount rate as an excuse for increasing the general interest rate to borrowers, and as a matter of fact they were encouraged to do so by the central bank and the government. In addition they were required by the central bank to maintain a special 7 per cent cash reserve over and above the 8 per cent normally required by the Bank of Canada.
This over-all credit restriction in itself has contributed to the wage-price spiral, in that it has imposed much heavier costs upon producers who have had to borrow for production purposes. It has been highly discriminatory right from the beginning. The big industry has had no trouble whatever getting the money it needed, and it is not having too much trouble today. However, the smaller industries, the little men, have been hardest hit and many of them have been forced out of business. Those Canadian people who have been trying to get homes for themselves-the little people again-have found it impossible during the past six months to borrow in order to get roofs over their heads. The home situation in Canada is serious and will likely be much more serious as the days go by and we bring in more immigrants. The small merchant, the individual enterpriser who has actually been the banker for many of the communities in Canada, has been forced into a desperate position as a consequence of the credit squeeze. The farmer has also been put in a very bad position.
I am sure that with enough time at my disposal it would be easy to prove that the over-all credit control effort by this government through the use of the discount rate and restriction of loans has been unjustified, has been wrong in principle and most ineffective. What the government has done in this respect has been likened to burning down the barn to kill the rat. Selective credit controls under the circumstances would have been perfectly justified and far more effective, selected in those areas wherein the trouble lay. Why in the world make everyone suffer because of those particular difficulties? But the government has not looked at it that way. The

The Address-Mr. Low
blanket credit control program put into effect by the governor of the Bank of Canada has discriminated against the little man, the individual enterpriser and the municipalities and provinces that have been so seriously affected by the government's policy.
The government ought to have learned that the mere tightening or loosening of the total volume of credit is not a cure-all for economic fluctuations. Over the years it should have been clear from our experience that the disastrous business cycle can be levelled out only through interrelation of government spending, taxes, savings, and investments, income, employment and money supply. If we are going to try to operate a full employment policy, then we must begin to bring our whole money system under the most careful and scientific management, not to leave it to Joe over in the Bank of Canada to set the policy and then follow along like a blind turkey. If we are going to try to operate with that full employment policy then we must bring our entire money system under close scrutiny and careful and scientific management.
I believe we now face the absolute necessity of the early appointment of a national finance and economic commission answerable directly to this parliament. Then this parliament should lay down for it a policy in specific terms and clothe it with authority to manage that policy. Nothing points out more strongly the real need for such a commission than the events of the past 14 or 15 years. In his state of the nation address last Saturday President Eisenhower suggested that he would ask congress to set up a similar commission for the United States. We Social Crediters have been advocating for many years the necessity of having a finance and economic commission clothed with the responsibilities I have mentioned. It seems to me it is time we did so in order that our efforts may be properly co-ordinated.
Nobody likes credit restrictions, that is true. I do not like them. However, it might be necessary under certain combinations of circumstances to apply selective credit controls in those particular branches of our economy where the trouble actually exists. I oppose most strongly the government's blanket credit control policy because it simply is not working, and it hits hardest the small business, the little fellow, the best and steadiest taxpayer we have in this country.
I think there is a lesson for all in the experience we are having at the present time. It is true that total volume of corporation profits looks big; percentage-wise it may not be so impressive. However, when we
see those swollen profits, rather than immediately demanding higher wages and salaries which can benefit only one section of the Canadian people at the expense of the others and at the same time force costs and therefore prices to go higher, would it not be better for us all to take the position that a fair share of those profits should be used to bring down costs and prices for everybody? It can be done. After all, it is not the level of wages and salaries that counts; it is the purchasing power we take home that matters. Our present inclination as a people seems to be to follow too eagerly the dog eat dog policy when for the sake of security and happiness we should follow the policy of live and help to live.
The rise in the cost of living can be successfully stopped without any serious interference with individual freedom, and it ought to be stopped; and the government must take immediate and strong action in this regard. However, the rest of us must be prepared to help; it is not a matter requiring only the effort of the government. I believe the federal government should allow a moderate increase in the money supply so as to bring down interest rates. That is indicated in every single aspect of our whole financial and economic situation. This moderate increase in the money supply could be used at this time to buy lower prices for the Canadian people through the use of the compensated price discount system which we have advocated for many years. Such a system will prevent increases in consumer prices but will not interfere in any way with adequate producer income.
I think, too, the government will have to be prepared to arrange for loans from the Bank of Canada to the provincial and municipal governments for those public works projects that are considered to be essential to the development of the provinces and their resources. These loans could be arranged at a rate of interest which would act as a stimulus for the downward interest trend that is so essential at this time.
I see, Mr. Speaker, my time is up. I have indicated only one of the harassing problems facing the Canadian people and with which the government is not coming to grips. I should have liked to deal with external affairs, agriculture and other important matters; there are at least 12 or 13 more. However, I am going to ask my colleagues to deal with them in the course of their contributions to this debate. They will be outlining the policies and program advocated by the Social Credit Association of Canada, and they will not be afraid to say positively what they would do in specific circumstances.

The Address-Mr. Low Let me say in conclusion that as a political organization in this country we place ourselves squarely and firmly on the side of the little fellow, the private enterpriser, the farmer, the small businessman, the Canadian consumer, and the home owner in the struggle for a better way of life, a freer way of life, under a policy of live and help to live that should apply within Canada as well as in our relations with other countries.

On motion of Mr. Cauchon the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: Statement by Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT AND DOCUMENTS RELATING TO RAILWAY STRIKE
speechtext:
,
In view of the widespread interest in the causes and effects of the work stoppage on the Canadian Pacific Railway Company system, not only in this house but in all parts of Canada, I think I should place on record a statement of the events leading up to the cessation of work at 4 p.m. on January 2 last.
The collective agreements between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company (eastern, prairie and Pacific regions including the Quebec Central Railway and Dominion Atlantic Railway) and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen, effective April 1, 1954, expired on March 31, 1956. Two months earlier, on February 1, the brotherhood served letters of notice on the managements of the eastern, prairie and Pacific regions of the railway and upon its subsidiaries for the revision of these agreements. On February 6 and 7, the company served similar notice on the brotherhood.
Representatives of the parties met in Toronto on February 21 and in Calgary on February 29 and negotiations between them continued up to April 18. On that date, the company requested me to establish a conciliation board to deal with the dispute and at the same time stated in detail its proposals for the revision of the collective agreements. On April 19, the brotherhood made the same request and likewise outlined its proposals for the revision of the agreement.
On the following day, April 20, 1956, I authorized a board of conciliation to be established and it was constituted as follows: His Honour Judge J. C. Anderson, Belleville, Ontario, chairman; Mr. Emmett M. Hall, Q.C., Saskatoon, and the honourable Senator Arthur W. Roebuck, Q.C., Toronto, nominees of the company and brotherhood respectively.
The brotherhood's proposals for changes in the collective agreement were as follows:
1.	Increase basic rates of pay in all classes of service by 25 per cent. All arbitraries, differentials and special allowances to be maintained and increased accordingly. Increased rates to be effective April 1, 1956.
2.	One full day's pay for each statutory holiday not worked. When service is performed during any part of a statutory holiday the entire day will be compensated for on the basis of time and one half the basic daily rate for the class of service concerned.
3.	Allowable service for pension purposes will accrue on the basis of all time in service.
The words "allowable service" will mean continuous relationships; absences for furlough or other reasons when seniority is unimpaired not to be deducted.
4.	A fireman or helper taken from the seniority ranks of locomotive firemen shall be employed on all motor cars used in road service and propelled by diesel, electric, gasoline, electricity or other power, and operated under the uniform code of operating rules by an engineer.
5.	Add to "mileage regulations": When a fireman is called for additional service out of his home terminal after he has attained the maximum mileage of 4,800 in passenger service or 3,800 in other service he will be paid at one and one half times the regular rate, double time where overtime is involved.
6.	Revise article 5, clause b (2) eastern region, article 5, clause b (5) prairie and Pacific regions as follows:
In the event of a fireman being deadheaded to an assignment at a station auxiliary to the main terminal, he is to be paid deadhead mileage in both directions to and from the main terminal. When assignments or runs are bulletined and no bids are received for positions at auxiliary terminals the junior firemen on the spare board at the main terminal will be required to man the assignment and will be paid deadhead mileage going to and returning from the assignment or run. The provisions of article 29 (q) will not be applicable to firemen who are required to deadhead from their home terminal to fill assignments or runs at points which are auxiliary to their divisional home terminal.
The company's proposals were as fohows: Firemen-System
1.	Eliminate all agreements, rules, regulations, interpretations or practices, however established, which require the employment or use of firemen (helpers) on other than steam power, and establish a rule to provide that the company shall have the unrestricted right to determine when and if a fireman (helper) shall be used on other than steam power.
2.	Eliminate all agreements, rules, regulations, interpretations or practices, however established, which provide rates of pay and daily earnings minima for firemen (helpers) on other than steam power, and establish a rule to provide that in instances where fireman (helper) is used on other than steam power a minimum rate of $7 per day of 100 miles shall apply.
3.	Eliminate preparatory and inspection time arbitraries and provide that firemen

Labour Conditions-C.P.R. Strike when employed will be paid for all time required to report for duty until released.
4.	Provide for initial terminal time payments in road service to be used to make up a short day on the same basis as final terminal time is now applied.
5.	Eliminate mountain and valley differentials.
The board held approximately 30 meetings between June 9, 1956, and November 25, 1956, all necessary adjournments in that period being made with the consent of the parties. The board's report submitted by His Honour Judge Anderson and Mr. Hall was received by me on December 18, 1956. A minority report submitted by Hon. Mr. Roebuck was received on the same date.
In summary, the report of the board contained the following recommendations:
1.	That the diesel rules be amended to permit the company to operate diesel engines in yard and freight service without firemen, with the understanding that if as a result of actual operating experience it appears that in some circumstances the services of the firemen might again be required, a modification of the rule might again be necessary and would then become the subject of further bargaining at a time when another agreement is being negotiated.
2.	That the company continue to employ all firemen who are at the date of the new agreement on the firemen's roster and who have passed their engineer's qualifications and/or attained three years of seniority as firemen.
3.	That the company give an undertaking to the brotherhood not to seek, when future contracts are open, the right to release these firemen from employment or to transfer them to other employment with the company where their direct line of promotion would not be to engineer, provided that the brotherhood at the same time gives an undertaking to the company which would provide that if at any time in the future it should agree to allow the Canadian National Railways to release from employment any or all of its firemen or to allow that railway to transfer to other employment any or all of its firemen, where the direct promotion is not to engineer, it would allow the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do likewise.
4.	That the parties to the dispute agree to set up a joint committee to discuss, decide and put into effect all plans, rules, details and procedures necessary to enable the company to carry out the new diesel rule.
5.	That the parties themselves discuss revisions of the present rules governing arbitra-ries relating to preparatory and inspection time and initial terminal time and that all mountain differentials be reduced to the
amount of the valley differentials but that the valley differentials be continued.
6.	That all wage rates applicable to miles, hours, overtime, arbitraries and special allowances be increased by 7 per cent effective April 1, 1956, and by a further 5 per cent effective June 1, 1957, and that the $4.25 per month per employee included in these increases subsequent to January 1, 1957, be in lieu of health and welfare benefits.
7.	That firemen in yard service be granted six statutory holidays with pay.
8.	That the pension proposal was clearly beyond the board's terms of reference.
9.	That the present rule relating to the operation of Budd cars remain unchanged.
10.	That the present rule governing mileage regulations remain unchanged.
In summary, the minority report recommended:
1.	That the present diesel rule in the collective agreements be not changed.
2.	That the company withdraw its proposal that firemen's pay on passenger diesel locomotive be reduced.
3.	That all present arbitraries be continued and that firemen be granted statutory holidays with pay on the same basis as now applying to trainmen.
4.	That a wage increase be granted as recommended in the report of the majority of the board.
5.	That the mileage regulations proposals be negotiated by the parties on the withdrawal by the company of its major proposal,
i.e., the removal of firemen on diesels in freight and yard service.
On December 20, my department was advised by the brotherhood that the recommendations of the board were not acceptable and on the following day, December 21, the company advised that it was prepared to accept and implement the recommendations of the board.
On the evening of Wednesday, December 26, a telegram (copy attached-Appendix "A") was received from Mr. W. E. Gamble, vice president of the brotherhood, advising that a strike vote by telegraph of the joint grievance committees of the brotherhood on the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Quebec Central Railway and Dominion Atlantic Railway, was unanimously in favour of strike action and that a withdrawal from railway service had been authorized, effective 4.00 p.m., January 2.
On Thursday, December 27, I discussed the whole matter with the Acting Prime Minister, Mr. Howe, and by telegram, I invited Mr. N. R. Crump, president of the company, and Mr. Gamble, Canadian vice

president of the brotherhood, to meet in Ottawa at 11.30 Saturday morning, December 29. (Copies attached-Appendix "B")
On Saturday morning and afternoon, December 29, the Acting Prime Minister, Mr. Howe, and I discussed the issues in dispute and methods of settlement with Mr. Crump and Mr. Gamble. The discussions revealed that the parties were adamant in their positions with respect to the employment of firemen on diesel locomotive in freight and yard service of the company. The company took the position that such employment was no longer necessary and the brotherhood was equally firm in holding that such employment was necessary both from the viewpoint of duties involved and the safety factor. The first meeting held on Saturday, was in the main exploratory in nature. No definite proposals were advanced by Mr. Howe or myself but the suggestion was made that the parties should consider a formula which would involve: (1) the union calling off the strike and the company withholding action on the removal of diesel firemen until:	(2) a joint union-company
committee with an independent chairman had given consideration to all aspects of the diesel issue: (3) in the meantime negotiations on other factors to continue. The parties were requested to consider this formula over Sunday and be prepared to discuss it more fully at the next meeting which was scheduled for Monday, Dec. 31.
The talks resumed at 10.00 a.m. on December 31 and, following morning and afternoon sessions, the Acting Prime Minister and myself announced that our efforts to obtain a settlement between the railway and the brotherhood had not succeeded. The discussions broke down on the diesel issue and both parties were unable to agree on the method by which this question should be resolved.	Mr. Gamble stated that the
brotherhood was willing to call off the strike and submit the diesel issue to a tribunal composed of company and union representatives, with an impartial chairman, the recommendations of such a body not to be binding on either party. Mr. Crump, for the company, on the other hand, desired that all issues in dispute be put before an impartial tribunal, for final determination binding on both parties.
Before dispersing, the parties were asked to give earnest consideration to the far-reaching and serious effects of the railway strike, more particularly in certain areas of Canada and on a large number of railway and other employees not directly affected by the dispute. At the same time they were advised that further mediation services would
Labour Conditions-C.P.R. Strike be made available if they were to reconsider their positions in the dispute.
On January 1, I telephoned both Mr. Gamble and Mr. Crump in order to see if they had altered their positions in any way and if the Department of Labour could be of further assistance to them but found no change in attitudes.
On January 2, the Acting Prime Minister addressed a telegram to Mr. Gamble and Mr. Crump (copies attached-Appendix "C") and received replies on January 3.
It had been made clear to both the parties to the dispute that the Department of Labour would be available if their services were required or in conveying any point of view from one side to the other, or for anything that might provide the basis of further negotiations.
The strike went into effect on 2nd January at 4 p.m.
On the afternoon of Friday, 4th January, I had a phone call from the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Claude Jodoin, asking me where I might be reached the following day, Saturday. I told him I would be at my office.
Late in the morning Saturday, 5th January,
I had a further phone call from Mr. Jodoin saying he had been having a meeting at his headquarters during the morning attended by his senior congress officials and by railway brotherhood officials. He asked if he and his two senior congress officers could come up to my office at once. I invited them to do so.
On arrival Mr. Jodoin told me that he was authorized to present a new proposal for settling the dispute.
Upon hearing this proposal I realized that it visualized a tribunal or commission of broader representation and scope than any that had been discussed by the two parties on the weekend before.
I reported this proposal to the Prime Minister and to the Right Hon. Mr. Howe on Saturday, 5th January.
The Prime Minister discussed the proposal by long distance with Mr. Crump in Montreal on Saturday evening.
Mr. Jodoin stated that he would ask the union leaders to remain in Ottawa over the week end or for as long as may be useful.
On Monday, 7th January, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress announced the Saturday proposals to the press, and sent me a copy of his press release thereon from which the proposal is set out attached in Appendix "D". On the same day the president of the C.P.R. announced that this proposal was not acceptable to the management.
